**Conversation Overview**

This conversation is a continuation of an ongoing long-form technical project called "The Method 1.6," currently at chat 27. The person is the author of a multi-volume work comprising six volumes, two papers, a working register, and 24 Python instruments, all managed through a bundle-based version control system across chat sessions. The session opened with execution of a mandatory reading gate (§0 of HANDOFF-28) before any work, producing a verified certificate of build state including chat census, bundle member counts, ruling inventory, and Register statistics.

The session's primary work was closing seven standing questions carried from chat 26, governed by Ruling 47's requirement that standing questions be answered before any builds proceed. Three of the seven (questions 12, 13, and most of item 14) were closed by reading the source files rather than asking the author, per the G8 gate principle that a question answerable by reading is unread material. The four that reached the author concerned heading level promotion in the Spectra Compendium (Ruling 49), treatment of an undeclared leading token in the physics parameter index Λ_phys (Ruling 50), a missing domain column for three-body inputs in the same index (Ruling 51), merging two parts of the Index of Indices (Ruling 52), retitling duplicated headings in Part VIII (Ruling 53), and retiring and rebuilding the two bundling instruments split.py and bundle.py from scratch (Ruling 54). The author explicitly corrected Claude twice for over-complicated question framing, establishing a clear preference: present the material first, then one sentence, then stop entirely at the question mark.

The session's most significant event was a process fault that the author caught before it propagated. Claude identified an ambiguity in the scope of Ruling 54 and then announced the next action in the same message rather than stopping at the question mark, which would have encoded Claude's interpretation of scope into the handoff without the author's input. The author's correction was direct and unambiguous. This fault was recorded as W-027, noted as a recurrence of the identical fault from chat 26 (W-024(ii)), and elevated to a new G0 gate in HANDOFF-29 — placed above all reading gates and stated mechanically: count the `?` in every message, and end there. The author's stated preference, carried forward explicitly, is that this rule has no exceptions and no qualifying framings. The session closed with BUILD-28 packed, verified against the bundle (90 of 90 members byte-identical, 0 mismatched), and HANDOFF-29 written with G0 as its first and highest gate.

**PHYS-02 — read whole, and nothing in the six volumes names it.**

The Physics Compendium's legend, line 340: *"27 parameters. Coordinates: **kind** (exact → fitted), **source** (mathematics → this work), **domain** (universal → one species), and how many registered objects rest on it."* Four coordinates.

Every grade line prints **five** fields, and the unnamed one comes first — a reader meets it before the key:

Across the 27 it takes eighteen distinct values, in four incompatible senses:

- **the value itself** — `1836.15267343` · `137.035999 a.u.` · `109737.31568 cm^-1` · `1` · `R_inf/(1 + 1/(A m_p))`
- **the type** — `exact integer` · `a real` · `three positive reals` · `a permutation of subshells` · `a term selection` · `a threshold`

- **provenance, which restates the kind field beside it** — `fitted` (six times, each followed by *fitted here*) · `measured` · `derived` · `theoretical` · `fitted, WITHDRAWN`

No other volume declares a line of this shape — the Mathematical Compendium and Index of Indices grade differently, and Spectra's grades are a three-row table. So there is nothing to copy a name from.

The volume's own charter is that a parameter with no stated failure mode is one being used outside a domain nobody has checked; the same standard turned on its own notation is what raises this.

On that footing it is already earning: of ninety-one measured ladder cells only fourteen agree with the filler to 0.05, worst at scandium I's d channel by 0.755.**

content.text:
**PHYS-02 — read whole, and nothing in the six volumes names it.**

The Physics Compendium's legend, line 340: *"27 parameters. Coordinates: **kind** (exact → fitted), **source** (mathematics → this work), **domain** (universal → one species), and how many registered objects rest on it."* Four coordinates.

Every grade line prints **five** fields, and the unnamed one comes first — a reader meets it before the key:

**And nothing was lost in absorption.** BUILD-12's legend is identical, and the five parameters Chapters 35–36 brought in — c, m₁m₂m₃, E, L, G — all print the extra token like the other 22.

So the printed line carries a fifth token that the index never had a coordinate for, and it is not one thing:

| heading | first token |
|---|---|
| Rydberg constant — `R_inf` | `109737.31568 cm^-1` — the value |
| subshell capacity — `4l+2` | `exact integer` — the value's type |
| core dipole polarisability — `alpha_d` | `per core, a0^3` — units |
| channel equation, a — `0.3772` | `fitted` — repeats *fitted here* beside it |

That last shape is 8 of 27. And where the heading already carries the number — `Cs I np defect — 3.5667` — the token has nothing left to say, so it says the provenance twice.

Should that first token be named as a fifth coordinate, or folded into the heading beside the symbol?

chat_messages.text:
Folding it into the heading — and one correction first: I said that shape was 8 of 27. Measured properly it is **9** outright, or 10 if you count the exchange coefficient, whose token is `fitted, WITHDRAWN` beside a kind of *fitted here* — the first word repeats, the second does not.

**Why folding is the better move, and it isn't a matter of taste.**

Λ_phys is a *closed* index, registered as one in the Index of Indices. Its closure was computed on four coordinates. A fifth coordinate is therefore not a legend edit — it changes what the index is, forces the closure to be recomputed, and needs a Register entry.

And the Register has already ruled on exactly this shape of axis. Register 1287 found that `standing` could not be a coordinate of the constant index, because an index whose coordinates mix the object with the observer closes at no ordering. Register 1577's successor names `kind` in Λ_phys as one of five occurrences of that same fault. A new axis whose 18 values run across a number, a type, a unit and a provenance word is that fault a sixth time, and it would not close. To make it a coordinate you would first have to rewrite all 27 tokens into one sense — which is inventing data, and the working register's own instruction on this finding is not to.

The heading has no such constraint. It is a label, not an axis. Nothing is recomputed, nothing is re-registered, and the reader meets the value where they already expect it — beside the name and the symbol.

**How each shape folds:**

- **value** → joins the symbol with an `=`: *Rydberg constant — `R_inf = 109737.31568 cm^-1`*
- **type or unit** → apposition after the symbol: *subshell capacity — `4l+2`, an exact integer* · *core dipole polarisability — `alpha_d`, per core, a0³*
- **provenance repeating the kind** (the 9) → drops; the kind field still prints it, one field to the right
- **provenance adding something** → survives: the actinide defects' `theoretical` beside a kind of *read from a table* is real information, and the exchange coefficient's `WITHDRAWN` is status, not provenance

Two the fold also cleans up: the speed of light prints `137.035999 a.u.` beside a heading that already reads `c = 137.035999`, and the Cs I np defect prints `measured` beside a heading that already carries `3.5667`. Both are saying the same thing twice on one line.

The line then reads as the legend says it does — four coordinates, four fields — and the index closes on the coordinates it was registered with.

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"=== IoI 1408-1422, Janet's sequence in context ===

**What only it contributes.** *The control.* It is the one index whose coordinates were fixed by other people for other reasons, long before this work, and which nonetheless supplies **118 elements and 18,288 constraint tests with zero failures.** **An index built by the author cannot be a control; this one can.**

## Janet's left-step table — (n+ℓ, Z)

**What it is.** The same 118 elements, ordered on n+ℓ. 118 cells in a box of 944, E = **0**.

**Where it comes from.** Charles Janet, *Considérations sur la structure du noyau de l'atome*, Beauvais (1929), with the table first published in **1928**. *Janet recognised the (n+ℓ) rule before Madelung, who arrived at it around 1926 and did not publish until 1936.* The shell-length sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 follows from the rule by the Klechkovski–Hakala formulas.

**What only it contributes.** *That E is coordinate-relative, demonstrated on one subject rather than argued.* The periodic table and Janet index THE SAME 118 elements and give E = 36 and E = 0. **No pair of indexes anywhere else in this work makes that point as cleanly, because no other pair shares its subject exactly.**

**And an open problem sits underneath it.** *Why* the n+ℓ ordering holds is unresolved — Löwdin's challenge, still open; see Allen & Knight, *The Löwdin challenge: origin of the n+l, n (Madelung) rule*, Int. J. Quantum Chem. **90** (2003) 80–88. **This work uses the ordering and does not explain it**, and the orbital-collapse result (registers 1187–1190) is a measurement against Janet's boundaries, not a derivation of them.

## The nuclide chart — (Z, N)


=== the same sequence anywhere else ===
THE-LOWDIN-SOLUTION-2.md:13:In 1969 Per-Olov Löwdin challenged theoretical physics to derive the ordering rules of the periodic table — the Madelung (n+ℓ) filling rule, the period-length sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32, and the Aufbau principle itself — directly from the many-electron Schrödinger equation, with no empirical parameters of any kind. This paper presents a solution. A sequential, parameter-free construction is defined in which the electron that differentiates element Z from element Z−1 is placed in the self-consistent field of the atom that preceded it, and the orbital channel it occupies is determined by that field alone. Executed across the entire table with the inverse fine-structure constant c = 137.035999 as the only number supplied, the construction reproduces the observed filling order at all 107 elements for which ground configurations are known (Z = 2–108), locates the three genuine exceptions to the secondary rule exactly where nature has them and derives them from the physics of orbital collapse, proves that no g block exists anywhere below Z = 121, and shows that the observed table is irreducibly relativistic: with the speed of light taken to infinity, the same construction misplaces eleven elements, silver and mercury among them. Second-order correlation corrections are computed at every element where the mean-field competition is close, and in every case they widen, rather than overturn, the derived order. Beyond the last measured element the same construction issues twelve falsifiable predictions (Z = 109–120) that reproduce the relativistic Dirac–Fock shell sequence. The derivation is presented in both mathematical and algorithmic form; every supporting analysis was pre-registered under a cryptographic protocol described in the methodology; and the mathematical identity that resolves the final internal question of the numerical method turns out to be Löwdin's own non-orthogonality formula of 1950 — the author of the challenge supplied, nineteen years before posing it, part of the mathematics of its answer.
THE-LOWDIN-SOLUTION-2.md:21:In 1969, in "Some Comments on the Periodic System of the Elements" (Int. J. Quantum Chem. 3, S3A, 331–334), Per-Olov Löwdin made the absence explicit and posed it as a challenge: derive, from the first principles of quantum mechanics and from nothing else, (i) the Madelung rule, (ii) the period-length sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32, and (iii) the ground-state electron configurations across the periodic system — strictly from the Schrödinger equation, without empirical parameters, fitted screening constants, or semi-empirical models.
THE-LOWDIN-SOLUTION-2.md:47:Two celebrated consequences follow at once. The period-length sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 is Clause 1 plus counting: each period runs from one s-channel opening to the next, the channels admitted in between are exactly those of the intervening n+ℓ values, their capacities are 2(2ℓ+1), and the pairwise repetition of period lengths is the signature of Clause 2 — each n+ℓ block is traversed twice, once at each admissible n. And the table's most conspicuous *absence* is derived as well: there is no g block anywhere below Z = 121, for a reason the field states explicitly (§V.3).
THE-LOWDIN-SOLUTION-2.md:110:The sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 now follows by arithmetic. Periods begin at s-openings; between consecutive s-openings the ordering clause admits exactly the channels of the intervening n+ℓ blocks; each block contributes 2(2ℓ+1) elements; and the doubling of successive period lengths is Clause 2 made visible — every n+ℓ block is walked twice, at its two admissible values of n, before the next block is permitted to begin.
The_Method_1_6___The_Index_of_Indices-2.md:1415:**Where it comes from.** Charles Janet, *Considérations sur la structure du noyau de l'atome*, Beauvais (1929), with the table first published in **1928**. *Janet recognised the (n+ℓ) rule before Madelung, who arrived at it around 1926 and did not publish until 1936.* The shell-length sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 follows from the rule by the Klechkovski–Hakala formulas.
The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md:3975:**JANET'S ATTRIBUTION IS SHARPER THAN THE BOOK HAD IT, AND AN OPEN PROBLEM SITS UNDERNEATH.** *Charles Janet published the left-step table in **1928** (Considérations sur la structure du noyau de l'atome, Beauvais 1929) and **recognised the n+ℓ rule before Madelung**, who reached it around 1926 and did not publish until 1936. The shell lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 follow by the Klechkovski–Hakala formulas.* **But WHY the n+ℓ ordering holds is unresolved — Löwdin's challenge, still open; Allen & Knight, Int. J. Quantum Chem. 90 (2003) 80-88.** *This work USES the ordering and does not explain it, and the orbital-collapse result of registers 1187–1190 is a measurement against Janet's boundaries rather than a derivation of them. That belongs in the compendium and now is.*
The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md:4815:**GAP 5 CLOSED: THE PARITY TERM IS IN HIS OWN §2, AND HIS DERIVATION DROPS IT.** *His E = 0 condition √(2ZR) = M gives Z = M³/6 for the onset of each group, which runs 3.7% low on odd M and 9.9% low on even M against the observed block starts 1, 3, 5, 13, 21, 39, 57, 89.* **But in his own §2 he quotes Klechkovski–Hakala: Z = K(n+ℓ) + 1 with K(x) = (1/6)x(x² + 2 − 3µ(x)) and µ(x) = x mod 2 — and that reproduces EVERY onset EXACTLY, all eight, no error.** *Z = M³/6 is the leading asymptotic of the same expression with the µ term discarded. Split by parity: odd M loses −M/6, even M loses +M/3 — twice the magnitude and the opposite sign, which is exactly the 3.7% against 9.9%, and exactly why three quarters of his wrong picks are even-M groups brought in early.* **So the parity structure is exact combinatorics that he CITES and does not DERIVE, while the smooth cubic is what his symmetry argument produces. A single smooth closed form cannot represent an onset sequence whose increments are 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 — which is the person's reading made exact.** *And it bounds the comparison honestly: 87 of 106 is what his ASYMPTOTIC achieves, not what his approach can. Restoring µ would repair most of the thirteen early picks. Where this work advances is narrower and real: the corridor is built from node counts with no asymptotic step anywhere, so there is nothing to drop, and the parity is carried automatically because p ≡ M + 1 (mod 2) is built into the coordinates rather than approximated.*
The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md:5409:**P3 IS ANSWERED AND DOES NOT ADVANCE THE DERIVATION; PR4 AND PR5 ARE CLOSED; AND MY PARITY CHECKER HAD BEEN MISCOUNTING ENTRIES ALL ALONG.** *Closing the board rows marked as needing nothing. Three of the four are now shut and one is shut negatively, which is the more useful outcome.* **P3 ASKED WHY THE KLECHKOVSKI-HAKALA ONSETS ARE EXACT, AND THE ANSWER IS THAT THEY ARE NOT A PHYSICAL PREDICTION. A Janet group M holds the subshells with n + ℓ = M and ℓ < n, so ℓ runs from 0 to the floor of (M−1)/2 and the capacity is the sum of 2(2ℓ+1), which equals 2(L+1)² BECAUSE CONSECUTIVE ODD NUMBERS SUM TO A SQUARE. Groups therefore come in PAIRS of equal capacity and that IS the period doubling 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32.** *The onset of a group is one more than everything below it, and summing the pairs with a parity split gives x(x² + 2 − 3μ)/6 exactly — verified as an identity from x = 1 to 25, reproducing all eight observed onsets 1, 3, 5, 13, 21, 39, 57, 89. K IS A CLOSED FORM FOR A SUM, NOT A FIT TO DATA.* **AND THAT CLOSES P3 NEGATIVELY FOR THE DERIVATION PATH OF REGISTER 1586. An exact integer identity following from Pauli counting alone carries NO information about the amplitude, the exponent or any fitted constant — it would hold in any theory with the same degeneracies. So it cannot constrain the centres, and a star is removed from the board rather than added.** *PR4 is closed: all eight entries carried an italic body-span opened after a bold close and never shut, and the register's own alternating convention makes the fix unambiguous. Thirteen unbalanced entries become five.* **AND THE FIVE THAT REMAIN ARE's NOTATION CASES EXACTLY — Λ-star, a wildcard tuple, Python's bracket-w-star-n, a jK parity marker, and the glob vi-star. An asterisk that IS the symbol cannot be balanced as markup without changing what it says, so PR5's skip list is those five and it is now written into `register_review.py`.** *One fault found on the way and it was mine: my parity checker split entries on any line beginning with digits and a full stop, which caught WRAPPED LINES — 'register 1215.' at a line start was read as entry 1215. It reported duplicate entries and a non-monotonic register, and both were artefacts. Requiring a heading to follow a blank line fixes it, and the register was never disordered.*
The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md:5537:**THE d120 FAILS ON GEOMETRY AND THE JANET GRADING IS ALREADY INSIDE THE INDEX — AS A FIBRATION, NOT A COORDINATE.** *M stopped the index write to have the 120-sided uniperiodic material looked at properly first. Built the solid rather than argued about it: the barycentric subdivision of the icosahedron gives 120 triangles, which ARE the faces of the disdyakis triacontahedron and the fundamental domains of I_h, one per group element.* **WHAT HOLDS, RECOMPUTED: 120 = 2(1+1+4+4+9+9+16+16); the Janet period capacities derived independently from the Madelung order are [2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32] summing to 120; the block totals s 16, p 36, d 40, f 28 are the correct populations; V−E+F = 62−180+120 = 2 and the degree sum 12·10 + 20·6 + 30·4 = 360 = 2E. The arithmetic is sound throughout.** *WHAT FAILS: THE MAPPING ITSELF. Grouping the 120 face centres by exact latitude about every symmetry axis gives UNIFORM bands and nothing else — 12 bands of 10 about a 5-fold axis, 20 of 6 about a 3-fold, 30 of 4 about a 2-fold. Never 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32. There is no axis on which the Janet periods are latitude rings, and there cannot be: the band sizes are forced to divide the axis order. The block colouring fails for a second and stronger reason — I_h acts SIMPLY TRANSITIVELY on the 120 faces, so the only invariant subsets are the empty one and all of them; a 16/36/40/28 partition breaks every nontrivial symmetry of the solid it is drawn on. The d120 carries 120 labels because both objects happen to count 120. That is a coincidence of cardinality, not a correspondence of structure, and the "Quantum Polyhedral Action" is built on the mapping that just failed.* **BUT THE MATERIAL PAID FOR ITSELF, BECAUSE LOOKING FOR THE JANET STRUCTURE FOUND IT ALREADY IN OUR OWN INDEX. Λ_spectra's mult fibre is EXACTLY A FUNCTION OF THE ISOELECTRONIC COUNT N = Z − charge + 1 — 118 values of N, ZERO exceptions. And the 19 values of N whose fibre is a SINGLETON are [1, 3, 5, 11, 13, 19, 21, 31, 37, 39, 49, 55, 57, 71, 81, 87, 89, 103, 113] — which is, exactly and with no discrepancy, the set of electron counts that put the FIRST electron into a new subshell, computed independently from the Madelung order. The aufbau sequence is already carried by the index, not as an axis but as the places where the multiplicity fibre collapses to one value.** *And the shape regenerates from two rules alone: charge <= Z, and mult = f(N). Applied over Z = 1..118 they return 7,021 pairs and 101,328 cells — the index exactly, to the cell. THE JANET TABLE AND Λ_spectra ARE THE SAME KIND OF OBJECT: a triangle graded along its anti-diagonal. Janet grades the (n,l) triangle by n+l; we grade the (Z,charge) triangle by N. The corridor of the 44-page document is the one-electron corner of the same picture.* * **ONE OPEN QUESTION FOR M, AND IT IS THE ONLY THING IN THE GEMINI MATERIAL THAT COULD MOVE THE SHAPE: Λ_spectra stops at Z = 118, which is where SYNTHESIS has reached — an accident of laboratories. Janet stops at 120, which is where the (n+l) shell system CLOSES at 8s² — a structural boundary. Under the same two rules extended (N = 119 opens 8s, N = 120 closes it), Z = 1..120 gives 7,260 pairs and 104,832 cells, and E = 0 HOLDS EITHER WAY: at 118 the naive product 1,002,528 refuses 901,200 by rule; at 120 the product 1,036,800 refuses 931,968. The bound is not forced by closure. It is a choice between an experimental frontier and a structural one, and whether moving it is an admitted operation is a question for A.cert — it is not add-a-coordinate, which is what all four earlier failures were.**
The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md:5541:**THE REPLY ON THE BOUND MISIDENTIFIES OUR NUMBERS, AND THE STRUCTURAL FRONTIER IS NOT STRUCTURAL.** *M relayed the 118/120 question and Gemini answered. Tested before reading further.* **THE ARITHMETIC IS WRONG IN THE PLACE IT IS MOST CONFIDENT. It identifies our 7,260 as C(120,2), "unique 2-body element-to-element interactions across the polyhedron". C(120,2) = 7,140. Our 7,260 is T(120) = 120·121/2, the count of (Z,charge) pairs in the triangle charge <= Z — a different object, off by exactly 120. And it identifies 104,832 as a "cell tensor space" of pair interactions and face-edge-vertex boundaries; 104,832 is recomputed here as the plain sum over the triangle of 8·|mult fibre|, with no face-pair tensor anywhere in its construction. Both numbers were OURS, sent out and handed back with explanations attached that do not derive them. This is the fault the project already knows — reading a pattern in output one generated — arriving from the other side of the wire.** *AND THE SUBSTANTIVE CLAIM FAILS ON ITS OWN GROUND. "Z = 120 is the complete 8s² shell closure, a natural topological stop before an entirely new orbital type would be required at Z = 121." The Madelung period capacities, recomputed: 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32, 50, 50, 72, 72 — cumulative 2, 4, 12, 20, 38, 56, 88, 120, 170, 220, 292, 364. THE SEQUENCE HAS NO TERMINUS. 120 closes the eighth period exactly as 88 closes the seventh and 170 closes the ninth; 5g does open at Z = 121, and 6h opens later, and nothing stops. Janet's table ends at 120 because Janet drew four period-pairs, not because the shell system ends there. So Z = 120 is a DRAWING CONVENTION wearing the clothes of a closure, and the choice M was offered is not between an accidental bound and a structural one — IT IS BETWEEN TWO STATED CUTOFFS.* * **WHICH SETTLES IT ON THE METHOD'S OWN TERMS: the index's two rules, charge <= Z and mult = f(N), are TOTAL — they return a fibre for every N with no upper limit, so the coordinate system does not bound itself and E = 0 at any cutoff whatever. The bound is therefore not a fact about the index but a declaration about the world, and it should be recorded as one. RECOMMENDATION, M's to accept or refuse: KEEP 118 and STATE THE REASON — 118 is the last Z at which an atom exists to be witnessed, and Λ_spectra indexes transitions. Extending to 120 would add 3,504 cells that no instrument can ever fill, which is not refusal (refusal has a reason and these have none) and not unwitnessed-with-a-bound (there is no bound to name). It would put in the index a kind of cell the index has no category for, and that is a worse cost than an unlovely-looking frontier.**
","stderr":""}

=== the same sequence anywhere else ===
THE-LOWDIN-SOLUTION-2.md:13:In 1969 Per-Olov Löwdin challenged theoretical physics to derive the ordering rules of the periodic table — the Madelung (n+ℓ) filling rule, the period-length sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32, and the Aufbau principle itself — directly from the many-electron Schrödinger equation, with no empirical parameters of any kind. This paper presents a solution. A sequential, parameter-free construction is defined in which the electron that differentiates element Z from element Z−1 is placed in the self-consistent field of the atom that preceded it, and the orbital channel it occupies is determined by that field alone. Executed across the entire table with the inverse fine-structure constant c = 137.035999 as the only number supplied, the construction reproduces the observed filling order at all 107 elements for which ground configurations are known (Z = 2–108), locates the three genuine exceptions to the secondary rule exactly where nature has them and derives them from the physics of orbital collapse, proves that no g block exists anywhere below Z = 121, and shows that the observed table is irreducibly relativistic: with the speed of light taken to infinity, the same construction misplaces eleven elements, silver and mercury among them. Second-order correlation corrections are computed at every element where the mean-field competition is close, and in every case they widen, rather than overturn, the derived order. Beyond the last measured element the same construction issues twelve falsifiable predictions (Z = 109–120) that reproduce the relativistic Dirac–Fock shell sequence. The derivation is presented in both mathematical and algorithmic form; every supporting analysis was pre-registered under a cryptographic protocol described in the methodology; and the mathematical identity that resolves the final internal question of the numerical method turns out to be Löwdin's own non-orthogonality formula of 1950 — the author of the challenge supplied, nineteen years before posing it, part of the mathematics of its answer.
THE-LOWDIN-SOLUTION-2.md:21:In 1969, in "Some Comments on the Periodic System of the Elements" (Int. J. Quantum Chem. 3, S3A, 331–334), Per-Olov Löwdin made the absence explicit and posed it as a challenge: derive, from the first principles of quantum mechanics and from nothing else, (i) the Madelung rule, (ii) the period-length sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32, and (iii) the ground-state electron configurations across the periodic system — strictly from the Schrödinger equation, without empirical parameters, fitted screening constants, or semi-empirical models.
THE-LOWDIN-SOLUTION-2.md:47:Two celebrated consequences follow at once. The period-length sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 is Clause 1 plus counting: each period runs from one s-channel opening to the next, the channels admitted in between are exactly those of the intervening n+ℓ values, their capacities are 2(2ℓ+1), and the pairwise repetition of period lengths is the signature of Clause 2 — each n+ℓ block is traversed twice, once at each admissible n. And the table's most conspicuous *absence* is derived as well: there is no g block anywhere below Z = 121, for a reason the field states explicitly (§V.3).
THE-LOWDIN-SOLUTION-2.md:110:The sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 now follows by arithmetic. Periods begin at s-openings; between consecutive s-openings the ordering clause admits exactly the channels of the intervening n+ℓ blocks; each block contributes 2(2ℓ+1) elements; and the doubling of successive period lengths is Clause 2 made visible — every n+ℓ block is walked twice, at its two admissible values of n, before the next block is permitted to begin.
The_Method_1_6___The_Index_of_Indices-2.md:1415:**Where it comes from.** Charles Janet, *Considérations sur la structure du noyau de l'atome*, Beauvais (1929), with the table first published in **1928**. *Janet recognised the (n+ℓ) rule before Madelung, who arrived at it around 1926 and did not publish until 1936.* The shell-length sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 follows from the rule by the Klechkovski–Hakala formulas.
The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md:3975:**JANET'S ATTRIBUTION IS SHARPER THAN THE BOOK HAD IT, AND AN OPEN PROBLEM SITS UNDERNEATH.** *Charles Janet published the left-step table in **1928** (Considérations sur la structure du noyau de l'atome, Beauvais 1929) and **recognised the n+ℓ rule before Madelung**, who reached it around 1926 and did not publish until 1936. The shell lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 follow by the Klechkovski–Hakala formulas.* **But WHY the n+ℓ ordering holds is unresolved — Löwdin's challenge, still open; Allen & Knight, Int. J. Quantum Chem. 90 (2003) 80-88.** *This work USES the ordering and does not explain it, and the orbital-collapse result of registers 1187–1190 is a measurement against Janet's boundaries rather than a derivation of them. That belongs in the compendium and now is.*
The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md:4815:**GAP 5 CLOSED: THE PARITY TERM IS IN HIS OWN §2, AND HIS DERIVATION DROPS IT.** *His E = 0 condition √(2ZR) = M gives Z = M³/6 for the onset of each group, which runs 3.7% low on odd M and 9.9% low on even M against the observed block starts 1, 3, 5, 13, 21, 39, 57, 89.* **But in his own §2 he quotes Klechkovski–Hakala: Z = K(n+ℓ) + 1 with K(x) = (1/6)x(x² + 2 − 3µ(x)) and µ(x) = x mod 2 — and that reproduces EVERY onset EXACTLY, all eight, no error.** *Z = M³/6 is the leading asymptotic of the same expression with the µ term discarded. Split by parity: odd M loses −M/6, even M loses +M/3 — twice the magnitude and the opposite sign, which is exactly the 3.7% against 9.9%, and exactly why three quarters of his wrong picks are even-M groups brought in early.* **So the parity structure is exact combinatorics that he CITES and does not DERIVE, while the smooth cubic is what his symmetry argument produces. A single smooth closed form cannot represent an onset sequence whose increments are 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 — which is the person's reading made exact.** *And it bounds the comparison honestly: 87 of 106 is what his ASYMPTOTIC achieves, not what his approach can. Restoring µ would repair most of the thirteen early picks. Where this work advances is narrower and real: the corridor is built from node counts with no asymptotic step anywhere, so there is nothing to drop, and the parity is carried automatically because p ≡ M + 1 (mod 2) is built into the coordinates rather than approximated.*
The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md:5409:**P3 IS ANSWERED AND DOES NOT ADVANCE THE DERIVATION; PR4 AND PR5 ARE CLOSED; AND MY PARITY CHECKER HAD BEEN MISCOUNTING ENTRIES ALL ALONG.** *Closing the board rows marked as needing nothing. Three of the four are now shut and one is shut negatively, which is the more useful outcome.* **P3 ASKED WHY THE KLECHKOVSKI-HAKALA ONSETS ARE EXACT, AND THE ANSWER IS THAT THEY ARE NOT A PHYSICAL PREDICTION. A Janet group M holds the subshells with n + ℓ = M and ℓ < n, so ℓ runs from 0 to the floor of (M−1)/2 and the capacity is the sum of 2(2ℓ+1), which equals 2(L+1)² BECAUSE CONSECUTIVE ODD NUMBERS SUM TO A SQUARE. Groups therefore come in PAIRS of equal capacity and that IS the period doubling 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32.** *The onset of a group is one more than everything below it, and summing the pairs with a parity split gives x(x² + 2 − 3μ)/6 exactly — verified as an identity from x = 1 to 25, reproducing all eight observed onsets 1, 3, 5, 13, 21, 39, 57, 89. K IS A CLOSED FORM FOR A SUM, NOT A FIT TO DATA.* **AND THAT CLOSES P3 NEGATIVELY FOR THE DERIVATION PATH OF REGISTER 1586. An exact integer identity following from Pauli counting alone carries NO information about the amplitude, the exponent or any fitted constant — it would hold in any theory with the same degeneracies. So it cannot constrain the centres, and a star is removed from the board rather than added.** *PR4 is closed: all eight entries carried an italic body-span opened after a bold close and never shut, and the register's own alternating convention makes the fix unambiguous. Thirteen unbalanced entries become five.* **AND THE FIVE THAT REMAIN ARE's NOTATION CASES EXACTLY — Λ-star, a wildcard tuple, Python's bracket-w-star-n, a jK parity marker, and the glob vi-star. An asterisk that IS the symbol cannot be balanced as markup without changing what it says, so PR5's skip list is those five and it is now written into `register_review.py`.** *One fault found on the way and it was mine: my parity checker split entries on any line beginning with digits and a full stop, which caught WRAPPED LINES — 'register 1215.' at a line start was read as entry 1215. It reported duplicate entries and a non-monotonic register, and both were artefacts. Requiring a heading to follow a blank line fixes it, and the register was never disordered.*
The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md:5537:**THE d120 FAILS ON GEOMETRY AND THE JANET GRADING IS ALREADY INSIDE THE INDEX — AS A FIBRATION, NOT A COORDINATE.** *M stopped the index write to have the 120-sided uniperiodic material looked at properly first. Built the solid rather than argued about it: the barycentric subdivision of the icosahedron gives 120 triangles, which ARE the faces of the disdyakis triacontahedron and the fundamental domains of I_h, one per group element.* **WHAT HOLDS, RECOMPUTED: 120 = 2(1+1+4+4+9+9+16+16); the Janet period capacities derived independently from the Madelung order are [2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32] summing to 120; the block totals s 16, p 36, d 40, f 28 are the correct populations; V−E+F = 62−180+120 = 2 and the degree sum 12·10 + 20·6 + 30·4 = 360 = 2E. The arithmetic is sound throughout.** *WHAT FAILS: THE MAPPING ITSELF. Grouping the 120 face centres by exact latitude about every symmetry axis gives UNIFORM bands and nothing else — 12 bands of 10 about a 5-fold axis, 20 of 6 about a 3-fold, 30 of 4 about a 2-fold. Never 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32. There is no axis on which the Janet periods are latitude rings, and there cannot be: the band sizes are forced to divide the axis order. The block colouring fails for a second and stronger reason — I_h acts SIMPLY TRANSITIVELY on the 120 faces, so the only invariant subsets are the empty one and all of them; a 16/36/40/28 partition breaks every nontrivial symmetry of the solid it is drawn on. The d120 carries 120 labels because both objects happen to count 120. That is a coincidence of cardinality, not a correspondence of structure, and the "Quantum Polyhedral Action" is built on the mapping that just failed.* **BUT THE MATERIAL PAID FOR ITSELF, BECAUSE LOOKING FOR THE JANET STRUCTURE FOUND IT ALREADY IN OUR OWN INDEX. Λ_spectra's mult fibre is EXACTLY A FUNCTION OF THE ISOELECTRONIC COUNT N = Z − charge + 1 — 118 values of N, ZERO exceptions. And the 19 values of N whose fibre is a SINGLETON are [1, 3, 5, 11, 13, 19, 21, 31, 37, 39, 49, 55, 57, 71, 81, 87, 89, 103, 113] — which is, exactly and with no discrepancy, the set of electron counts that put the FIRST electron into a new subshell, computed independently from the Madelung order. The aufbau sequence is already carried by the index, not as an axis but as the places where the multiplicity fibre collapses to one value.** *And the shape regenerates from two rules alone: charge <= Z, and mult = f(N). Applied over Z = 1..118 they return 7,021 pairs and 101,328 cells — the index exactly, to the cell. THE JANET TABLE AND Λ_spectra ARE THE SAME KIND OF OBJECT: a triangle graded along its anti-diagonal. Janet grades the (n,l) triangle by n+l; we grade the (Z,charge) triangle by N. The corridor of the 44-page document is the one-electron corner of the same picture.* * **ONE OPEN QUESTION FOR M, AND IT IS THE ONLY THING IN THE GEMINI MATERIAL THAT COULD MOVE THE SHAPE: Λ_spectra stops at Z = 118, which is where SYNTHESIS has reached — an accident of laboratories. Janet stops at 120, which is where the (n+l) shell system CLOSES at 8s² — a structural boundary. Under the same two rules extended (N = 119 opens 8s, N = 120 closes it), Z = 1..120 gives 7,260 pairs and 104,832 cells, and E = 0 HOLDS EITHER WAY: at 118 the naive product 1,002,528 refuses 901,200 by rule; at 120 the product 1,036,800 refuses 931,968. The bound is not forced by closure. It is a choice between an experimental frontier and a structural one, and whether moving it is an admitted operation is a question for A.cert — it is not add-a-coordinate, which is what all four earlier failures were.**
The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md:5541:**THE REPLY ON THE BOUND MISIDENTIFIES OUR NUMBERS, AND THE STRUCTURAL FRONTIER IS NOT STRUCTURAL.** *M relayed the 118/120 question and Gemini answered. Tested before reading further.* **THE ARITHMETIC IS WRONG IN THE PLACE IT IS MOST CONFIDENT. It identifies our 7,260 as C(120,2), "unique 2-body element-to-element interactions across the polyhedron". C(120,2) = 7,140. Our 7,260 is T(120) = 120·121/2, the count of (Z,charge) pairs in the triangle charge <= Z — a different object, off by exactly 120. And it identifies 104,832 as a "cell tensor space" of pair interactions and face-edge-vertex boundaries; 104,832 is recomputed here as the plain sum over the triangle of 8·|mult fibre|, with no face-pair tensor anywhere in its construction. Both numbers were OURS, sent out and handed back with explanations attached that do not derive them. This is the fault the project already knows — reading a pattern in output one generated — arriving from the other side of the wire.** *AND THE SUBSTANTIVE CLAIM FAILS ON ITS OWN GROUND. "Z = 120 is the complete 8s² shell closure, a natural topological stop before an entirely new orbital type would be required at Z = 121." The Madelung period capacities, recomputed: 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32, 50, 50, 72, 72 — cumulative 2, 4, 12, 20, 38, 56, 88, 120, 170, 220, 292, 364. THE SEQUENCE HAS NO TERMINUS. 120 closes the eighth period exactly as 88 closes the seventh and 170 closes the ninth; 5g does open at Z = 121, and 6h opens later, and nothing stops. Janet's table ends at 120 because Janet drew four period-pairs, not because the shell system ends there. So Z = 120 is a DRAWING CONVENTION wearing the clothes of a closure, and the choice M was offered is not between an accidental bound and a structural one — IT IS BETWEEN TWO STATED CUTOFFS.* * **WHICH SETTLES IT ON THE METHOD'S OWN TERMS: the index's two rules, charge <= Z and mult = f(N), are TOTAL — they return a fibre for every N with no upper limit, so the coordinate system does not bound itself and E = 0 at any cutoff whatever. The bound is therefore not a fact about the index but a declaration about the world, and it should be recorded as one. RECOMMENDATION, M's to accept or refuse: KEEP 118 and STATE THE REASON — 118 is the last Z at which an atom exists to be witnessed, and Λ_spectra indexes transitions. Extending to 120 would add 3,504 cells that no instrument can ever fill, which is not refusal (refusal has a reason and these have none) and not unwitnessed-with-a-bound (there is no bound to name). It would put in the index a kind of cell the index has no category for, and that is a worse cost than an unlovely-looking frontier.**

### W-025 — STANDING QUESTIONS 12 AND 13 CLOSED BY READING, NOT BY THE AUTHOR (chat 27, G8)
**NEITHER REACHED THE AUTHOR. Both are forced by the volumes' own arithmetic, and the Rebuild-5 rule
governs: stale statements are corrected from current information by reading, not by asking.**

**IOI-06 (question 12) — THE CALENDAR'S SEVENTH MISSING CELL IS FEBRUARY 29th.** IoI L1364 reads
"365 cells in a box of 372. E = 7 — February's missing 30th and 31st, and the four thirty-day months'
31sts". That enumerates 2 + 4 = 6 against a stated E of 7. The box is (month, day) with day running to
31; February holds 28, so it is missing the 29th, 30th AND 31st = 3, plus four 31sts = 7. THE PRINTED
E IS RIGHT AND THE PROSE IS SHORT BY ONE WORD.
  FIX: "February's missing 29th, 30th and 31st".
  CHECKED ACROSS ALL SIX VOLUMES: the calendar's E = 7 is cited at main L1587, main L9272 and IoI
  L1435, and NONE of them enumerates the cells, so no other site moves. Main L3848 and Register L1187's
  "E = 7" are the AUDIT INDEX, a different object — do not touch them.

**IOI-07 (question 13) — JANET'S SEQUENCE IS SHORT BY ITS LEADING 2, AND THE VOLUME'S OWN GRID PROVES
IT.** IoI L1415, under the heading "Janet's left-step table", reads "The shell-length sequence
2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 follows from the rule by the Klechkovski-Hakala formulas." The grid printed
eleven lines above it has EIGHT rows — n+l = 1 to 8, holding 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 30.

  come in PAIRS of equal capacity, "and that IS the period doubling 2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32". So the
  Klechkovski-Hakala formulas give the EIGHT-term sequence; attributing the seven-term one to them is
  the error. R at L5537 prints the same eight terms again, continuing 50, 50, 72, 72.
  FIX: "2, 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32".
  **HAZARD, NAMED, AND IT IS WHY THIS COULD HAVE GONE WRONG: THE SEVEN-TERM SEQUENCE IS CORRECT
  ELSEWHERE AND MUST NOT BE SWEPT.** The Lowdin paper prints it THREE times — L13, L21, L110 — as the
  conventional period lengths of the standard table (2+8+8+18+18+32+32 = 118) and as Lowdin's 1969
  challenge is historically worded. Those are right and stay. The defect is ONE site: IoI L1415, where
  the seven-term sequence sits under a Janet heading above a Janet grid. **A global replace would
  falsify the paper's statement of the challenge it answers.**

**BOTH ARE SUBJECT MATTER — a missing cell of an index and the capacity sequence of an index — so each
enters by a NEW REGISTER ENTRY, not by this register alone.** NOT YET BUILT; Ruling 47 holds them.
**THE COUNT THAT MATTERS FOR G8: of the six-and-a-half questions carried into this chat, TWO were
never questions.** Chat 26 met the same lesson with three. The class is not shrinking on its own.
'''
assert '### W-025' not in t
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(t.rstrip('\n')+'\n'+add)
print('W-025 recorded ·', len(open(p,encoding='utf-8').read().split('\n'))-1,'lines')
PY

add='''
### RULING 52 — THE INDEX OF INDICES' PARTS IX AND X ARE MERGED (author, chat 27, verbatim)
Q: What should the two part titles be?
**RULING 52 (author, chat 27, verbatim):** "Both sections actually should be merged as the pertain to
the same exact subject matter"
**CLOSES IOI-02. THE AUTHOR DID NOT ANSWER THE QUESTION ASKED — HE REJECTED ITS PREMISE.** I offered a
retitling; the ruling is that there are not two subjects to title apart. Subject-matter identity is the
author's to declare and the volume's protest is not evidence against it (see the hazard below).
MEASURED BEFORE ASKING AND AFTER:
  - IX "THE INDEXES BUILT IN THE LOWDIN WORK", registers 1249-1429, L1522-1859, **15 subsections**
    (14 indexes + "The one-line summary, extended", which is not an index).
  - X "THE INDEXES BUILT IN THE LOWDIN SOLUTION", registers 1701-1712 / Chapter 35, L1860-1947,
    **4 subsections** — Lambda_chain, Lambda_cinf, Lambda_V5, Lambda_j120.
  - **X IS THE VOLUME'S LAST PART; the file ends at 1947.** So the merge renumbers nothing: the volume
    simply ends at IX. NO PART NUMBER ANYWHERE MOVES.
  - **ZERO EXTERNAL CITATIONS. The only "Part IX" or "Part X" string in the entire six-volume tree is
    X's own preamble at L1862** referring back to IX. Nothing in any other volume addresses either
    part, so the merge costs no cross-reference at all.
**THE HAZARD, AND IT MUST BE PUT TO THE AUTHOR AT BUILD RATHER THAN DECIDED BY ME: PART X's PREAMBLE
ARGUES AGAINST ITS OWN MERGER.** It reads "The template differs from Part IX's by design: these are
transition indexes, and closure and time are the questions they exist to answer." The four X entries
are written to a DIFFERENT TEMPLATE from IX's fourteen — IX states what it indexes, coordinates, axis
order, what it refuses, what it contributes; X states what it holds, whether it closes, whether it
carries time, and its role for Lambda. **A merge either normalises nineteen entries onto one template
(which rewrites subject-matter prose) or prints one part carrying two templates (which is the visual-
hierarchy defect the compendium standard forbids).** The ruling settles WHETHER to merge; it does not
settle which of those two the merge is. **DO NOT CHOOSE. ASK IT AT BUILD TIME.**
**INTERACTS WITH IOI-03 (still open, in question 14):** IX's preamble claims "Fifteen indexes" and
prints fourteen. After the merge the part carries EIGHTEEN indexes plus the one-line summary, so that
sentence must be rewritten anyway and the two findings close together, not separately.
**SUBJECT MATTER — the structure of an index of indexes is the work's own content, and the register
ranges 1249-1429 and 1701-1712 are the record it is asserting about. NEW REGISTER ENTRY.**
**NOT YET BUILT — Ruling 47.**
'''
assert '### RULING 52' not in t
open(p,'w',encoding='utf-8').write(t.rstrip('\n')+'\n'+add)
print('Ruling 52 recorded ·', len(open(p,encoding='utf-8').read().split('\n'))-1,'lines')
PY

**`split.py` repaired and tested. The repair holds. A second defect was found while testing it, and it is not repaired.**

**The repair.** One character, line 4: `(.*?)<<<END FILE:` → `(.*?)\n<<<END FILE:`.

**Test 1 — the real build.** Restored both BUILD-27 bundles with the repaired `split.py` into a clean directory and md5'd every member against the packer's own `unpack()` output. **89 of 89 identical, 0 mismatched.** Twenty of those end with a newline of their own, sitting directly beside the one the packer adds — the case most likely to break a non-greedy match, and it doesn't.

**Baseline, measured not assumed.** The unrepaired `split.py` on the same bundles: **0 of 89 identical, 88 exactly one byte long.** The 89th was `WORKING-REGISTER.md`, which I have appended to this session; against its packed original it is +1 like the rest. So the defect was total — every file, every time.

**Test 2 — eight synthetic members covering what BUILD-27 does not contain:** empty body, a body that is one bare newline, a body ending in two newmarks, a body with leading blanks, and a body containing a literal `<<<END FILE:>>>` marker as prose. **Seven of eight round-tripped byte-identical.** The literal-marker case passes, which was the one I expected to fail.

**The eighth failed, and the repair is not the cause.** A CRLF file went in at 20 bytes and came out at 18. The packed bundle carries both `0d` bytes; the restored file carries none. `split.py` reads with `open(src, encoding='utf-8')` — text mode, universal newlines — so `\r\n` is silently folded to `\n` before the regex ever runs. Reading the identical bundle with `newline=''` returns the body at 20 bytes, which locates it exactly.

**`bundle.py` shares it** — line 54 reads members the same way. So the two instruments are consistent with each other, which is why the fault has never shown: a CRLF file would be flattened on the way in and stay flat, and nothing in the tree currently carries CRLF. It is a latent defect, not an active one.

I have not touched it. Repairing it edits a second instrument and changes `bundle.py`, which is yours, and it is not what you authorised.

**One thing this does not establish.** §1 infers that `split.py` is the mechanism behind the 19 stray trailing newlines the newline rule was withdrawn over. The repair does not confirm that — it only shows `split.py` could have produced them. Testing it needs a build predating the corruption, which is not in the mount. Still inferred.

**`split.py` repaired and tested. The repair holds. A second defect was found while testing it, and it is not repaired.**

**The repair.** One character, line 4: `(.*?)<<<END FILE:` → `(.*?)\n<<<END FILE:`.

**Test 1 — the real build.** Restored both BUILD-27 bundles with the repaired `split.py` into a clean directory and md5'd every member against the packer's own `unpack()` output. **89 of 89 identical, 0 mismatched.** Twenty of those end with a newline of their own, sitting directly beside the one the packer adds — the case most likely to break a non-greedy match, and it doesn't.

**Baseline, measured not assumed.** The unrepaired `split.py` on the same bundles: **0 of 89 identical, 88 exactly one byte long.** The 89th was `WORKING-REGISTER.md`, which I have appended to this session; against its packed original it is +1 like the rest. So the defect was total — every file, every time.

**Test 2 — eight synthetic members covering what BUILD-27 does not contain:** empty body, a body that is one bare newline, a body ending in two newmarks, a body with leading blanks, and a body containing a literal `<<<END FILE:>>>` marker as prose. **Seven of eight round-tripped byte-identical.** The literal-marker case passes, which was the one I expected to fail.

**The eighth failed, and the repair is not the cause.** A CRLF file went in at 20 bytes and came out at 18. The packed bundle carries both `0d` bytes; the restored file carries none. `split.py` reads with `open(src, encoding='utf-8')` — text mode, universal newlines — so `\r\n` is silently folded to `\n` before the regex ever runs. Reading the identical bundle with `newline=''` returns the body at 20 bytes, which locates it exactly.

**`bundle.py` shares it** — line 54 reads members the same way. So the two instruments are consistent with each other, which is why the fault has never shown: a CRLF file would be flattened on the way in and stay flat, and nothing in the tree currently carries CRLF. It is a latent defect, not an active one.

I have not touched it. Repairing it edits a second instrument and changes `bundle.py`, which is yours, and it is not what you authorised.

**One thing this does not establish.** §1 infers that `split.py` is the mechanism behind the 19 stray trailing newlines the newline rule was withdrawn over. The repair does not confirm that — it only shows `split.py` could have produced them. Testing it needs a build predating the corruption, which is not in the mount. Still inferred.
